## Overview

The `qte` package provides seven estimators of the quantile treatment effect
on the treated (QTT) for settings where units are observed before and after
treatment. All share the same `yname`/`gname`/`tname`/`idname` interface and
support staggered treatment adoption. They differ in their identifying
assumptions. Six are difference-in-differences-type assumptions, which
restrict how untreated outcomes change over time; one, `lou_qtt()`, is a
selection-on-observables assumption that conditions on the lagged outcome.

This vignette states each assumption and shows the minimal call. For the full
applied workflow (aggregations, event studies, testing whether the effect is
more than a location shift, covariates), see `vignette("staggered-adoption")`.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
library(qte)
library(ptetools)
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(42)
data(mpdta, package = "did")
```

```{r}
#| label: compute-results
#| include: false
# Results are precomputed and cached so CRAN's vignette rebuild doesn't have
# to re-run the bootstrap on every check. Delete
# precomputed/panel-estimators-results.rds and re-render to regenerate after
# a code change (see CLAUDE.md).
cache_file <- "precomputed/panel-estimators-results.rds"
use_cache <- file.exists(cache_file)

fit <- function(estimator) {
  estimator(
    yname  = "lemp", gname = "first.treat", tname = "year",
    idname = "countyreal", data = mpdta,
    gt_type = "qtt", probs = seq(0.1, 0.9, 0.1), biters = 100
  )
}

if (use_cache) {
  cached <- readRDS(cache_file)
} else {
  cached <- list(
    res_cic  = fit(cic),
    res_qdid = fit(qdid),
    res_pqtt = fit(panel_qtt),
    res_ddid = fit(ddid),
    res_mdid = fit(mdid),
    res_cdf  = fit(cdf_did),
    res_lou  = fit(lou_qtt)
  )
  saveRDS(cached, cache_file)
}
list2env(cached, envir = environment())
```

We use `mpdta` throughout: a balanced panel of 500 US counties observed
annually from 2003–2007, with `lemp` (log employment) as the outcome and
`first.treat` as the cohort variable (year of first minimum wage increase; 0
= never treated).

The common call structure for all seven estimators is:

```r
estimator(
  yname  = "lemp",        # outcome
  gname  = "first.treat", # first treatment period (0 = never treated)
  tname  = "year",        # calendar time
  idname = "countyreal",  # unit id
  data   = mpdta,
  gt_type = "qtt",        # "qtt" (QTT curve) or "att"
  probs   = seq(0.1, 0.9, 0.1),
  biters  = 100
)
```

With `gt_type = "qtt"`, each estimator returns the QTT curve together with
the ATT implied by the same assumption, both from the same bootstrap draws.
Each plot below shows the overall QTT curve with a uniform confidence band
and the overall ATT as a horizontal line.

All of these estimators except `cdf_did()` are built on quantiles or ranks
and are designed for continuous outcomes. With a discrete outcome, or one
with a large mass point (such as many zeros), quantile treatment effects are
usually not point identified, and the estimators warn.

---

## Change in Changes — `cic()`

**Reference:** @athey-imbens-2006

**Identifying assumption:** The distributional time-change is the same for both groups:
$$Q_{Y_t(0)|D=1}\!\left(F_{Y_{t-1}(0)|D=1}(y)\right) = Q_{Y_t(0)|D=0}\!\left(F_{Y_{t-1}(0)|D=0}(y)\right) \quad \text{for all } y,$$
along with a support condition: $\text{supp}(Y_{t-1}(0)|D=1) \subseteq \text{supp}(Y_{t-1}(0)|D=0)$.

**Intuition:** The expression $Q_{Y_t(0)|D=g}(F_{Y_{t-1}(0)|D=g}(y))$ takes a pre-period value $y$, finds its quantile rank in group $g$'s pre-period distribution, and returns the post-period value at that same rank within group $g$'s distribution. The assumption requires this operation to give the same result for both groups at every $y$. It can be thought of as a nonlinear version of parallel trends: where parallel trends requires the *mean* of $Y(0)$ to shift equally across groups, CiC requires the *entire distributional time-change* to be the same. @athey-imbens-2006 derive it from a model $Y(0) = h(U, t)$ with $h$ increasing in unobservables $U$ whose distribution does not change over time within a group.

**Identification:** Under this assumption the counterfactual quantile function is
$$Q_{Y_t(0)|D=1}(\tau) = Q_{Y_t|D=0}\!\left(F_{Y_{t-1}|D=0}\!\left(Q_{Y_{t-1}|D=1}(\tau)\right)\right).$$

**Data:** Panel data or repeated cross sections (`panel = FALSE`).

```{r}
#| label: cic
#| eval: false
res_cic <- cic(
  yname  = "lemp", gname = "first.treat", tname = "year",
  idname = "countyreal", data = mpdta,
  gt_type = "qtt", probs = seq(0.1, 0.9, 0.1), biters = 100
)
autoplot(res_cic)
```

```{r}
#| label: cic-plot
#| echo: false
#| fig-alt: "Overall QTT curve from cic()"
autoplot(res_cic)
```

---

## Quantile Difference-in-Differences — `qdid()`

**References:** @athey-imbens-2006; @meyer-viscusi-durbin-1995

**Identifying assumption:** The change in quantiles over time is the same for both groups:
$$Q_{Y_t(0)|D=1}(\tau) - Q_{Y_{t-1}(0)|D=1}(\tau) = Q_{Y_t(0)|D=0}(\tau) - Q_{Y_{t-1}(0)|D=0}(\tau) \quad \text{for all } \tau \in (0,1).$$

**Intuition:** This requires parallel trends to hold at every quantile level $\tau$, not just in the mean. It directly identifies the counterfactual:
$$Q_{Y_t(0)|D=1}(\tau) = Q_{Y_{t-1}|D=1}(\tau) + Q_{Y_t|D=0}(\tau) - Q_{Y_{t-1}|D=0}(\tau).$$

**Data:** Panel data or repeated cross sections (`panel = FALSE`).

```{r}
#| label: qdid
#| eval: false
res_qdid <- qdid(
  yname  = "lemp", gname = "first.treat", tname = "year",
  idname = "countyreal", data = mpdta,
  gt_type = "qtt", probs = seq(0.1, 0.9, 0.1), biters = 100
)
autoplot(res_qdid)
```

```{r}
#| label: qdid-plot
#| echo: false
#| fig-alt: "Overall QTT curve from qdid()"
autoplot(res_qdid)
```

---

## Panel QTT — `panel_qtt()`

**Reference:** @callaway-li-2019

**Identifying assumptions:** The first assumption is $\Delta Y_t(0) \perp D$ — the distribution of the change in untreated potential outcomes is the same for both groups:
$$F_{\Delta Y_t(0)|D=1} = F_{\Delta Y_t(0)|D=0}.$$
This identifies the marginal distribution of $\Delta Y_t(0)$ for the treated group. As shown in @fan-yu-2012, this is not sufficient on its own to identify the QTT. Identification is completed by a copula stability assumption: the copula linking $\Delta Y_t(0)$ to the lagged outcome $Y_{t-1}(0)$ is stable over time within the treated group,
$$C_{\Delta Y_t(0),\, Y_{t-1}(0)|D=1} = C_{\Delta Y_{t-1}(0),\, Y_{t-2}(0)|D=1}.$$

**Intuition:** For treated units, $Y_{t-1}$ and $Y_{t-2}$ are observed pre-treatment, so the right-hand copula can be estimated directly from the data. Copula stability says this same dependence structure governs $(\Delta Y_t(0), Y_{t-1}(0))$ in the post-period. Combined with the identified marginals, this pins down the conditional distribution of $\Delta Y_t(0)$ given $Y_{t-1}(0) = y$ for treated units. Since $Y_t(0) = Y_{t-1} + \Delta Y_t(0)$ and $Y_{t-1}$ is observed, the QTT is identified.

**Data:** Panel data, with at least two pre-treatment periods per cohort.
With staggered adoption, the default `pre_copula = "long"` uses a
pre-treatment window as long as the post-treatment horizon, so longer event
times need more pre-treatment periods; `pre_copula = "short"` always uses the
two periods just before treatment.

```{r}
#| label: panel-qtt
#| eval: false
res_pqtt <- panel_qtt(
  yname  = "lemp", gname = "first.treat", tname = "year",
  idname = "countyreal", data = mpdta,
  gt_type = "qtt", probs = seq(0.1, 0.9, 0.1), biters = 100
)
autoplot(res_pqtt)
```

```{r}
#| label: panel-qtt-plot
#| echo: false
#| fig-alt: "Overall QTT curve from panel_qtt()"
autoplot(res_pqtt)
```

---

## Distributional DiD — `ddid()`

**Reference:** @callaway-li-2019

**Identifying assumptions:** The first is $\Delta Y_t(0) \perp D$ — the same as in `panel_qtt()`. The copula assumption differs: rather than stability over time, `ddid()` assumes the copula of $(\Delta Y_t(0), Y_{t-1}(0))$ is the same for treated and untreated groups,
$$C_{\Delta Y_t(0),\, Y_{t-1}(0)|D=1} = C_{\Delta Y_t(0),\, Y_{t-1}(0)|D=0}.$$

**Intuition:** For the untreated group, $\Delta Y_t(0) = \Delta Y_t$ is observed, so the right-hand copula can be estimated directly. The assumption transfers it to the treated group. Combined with the identified marginals, this pins down the joint distribution of $(\Delta Y_t(0), Y_{t-1}(0))$ for treated units and identifies the QTT — in exactly the same way as `panel_qtt()`. The key contrast is the source of the copula: `ddid()` borrows it from the untreated group at the same point in time, while `panel_qtt()` borrows it from the treated group's own pre-treatment history.

**Data:** Panel data, with one pre-treatment period per cohort.

```{r}
#| label: ddid
#| eval: false
res_ddid <- ddid(
  yname  = "lemp", gname = "first.treat", tname = "year",
  idname = "countyreal", data = mpdta,
  gt_type = "qtt", probs = seq(0.1, 0.9, 0.1), biters = 100
)
autoplot(res_ddid)
```

```{r}
#| label: ddid-plot
#| echo: false
#| fig-alt: "Overall QTT curve from ddid()"
autoplot(res_ddid)
```

---

## Mean Difference-in-Differences — `mdid()`

**Reference:** @thuysbaert-2007

**Identifying assumption:** The counterfactual quantile for the treated group in the post-period is the pre-period quantile shifted by the mean change in outcomes for the untreated group:
$$Q_{Y_t(0)|D=1}(\tau) = Q_{Y_{t-1}|D=1}(\tau) + E[Y_t|D=0] - E[Y_{t-1}|D=0].$$

**Intuition:** The assumption says the shape of the treated group's outcome distribution is unchanged in the counterfactual — the entire distribution simply shifts by the amount the untreated group's mean changed. This implies mean parallel trends, so the ATT is the usual DiD estimate, but it is stronger: it additionally requires that only the location of the untreated distribution changes over time, not its shape.

**Data:** Panel data or repeated cross sections (`panel = FALSE`).

```{r}
#| label: mdid
#| eval: false
res_mdid <- mdid(
  yname  = "lemp", gname = "first.treat", tname = "year",
  idname = "countyreal", data = mpdta,
  gt_type = "qtt", probs = seq(0.1, 0.9, 0.1), biters = 100
)
autoplot(res_mdid)
```

```{r}
#| label: mdid-plot
#| echo: false
#| fig-alt: "Overall QTT curve from mdid()"
autoplot(res_mdid)
```

## Parallel Trends in Distribution Functions — `cdf_did()`

**Reference:** @roth-santanna-2021

**Identifying assumption:** The change over time in the distribution function of untreated potential outcomes is the same for both groups, at every value $y$:
$$F_{Y_t(0)|D=1}(y) - F_{Y_{t-1}(0)|D=1}(y) = F_{Y_t(0)|D=0}(y) - F_{Y_{t-1}(0)|D=0}(y) \quad \text{for all } y.$$

**Intuition:** This is parallel trends for every indicator $1\{Y \le y\}$
instead of for $Y$ itself. @roth-santanna-2021 show that it is essentially
the condition under which parallel trends holds for every strictly monotone
transformation of the outcome (logs, levels, ...), so it is the natural
assumption when the choice of units is arbitrary. It implies mean parallel
trends, so the ATT is the usual DiD estimate. The counterfactual
distribution is
$$F_{Y_t(0)|D=1}(y) = F_{Y_{t-1}|D=1}(y) + F_{Y_t|D=0}(y) - F_{Y_{t-1}|D=0}(y).$$
In finite samples the right-hand side need not be a valid distribution
function; `cdf_did()` rearranges it into one [@chernozhukov-val-galichon-2010]
and reports how much that changed it.

Unlike the rank- and quantile-based estimators above, this assumption
identifies the counterfactual distribution for discrete outcomes too. With
covariates, `est_method = c("aipw", "ipw", "reg")` gives doubly robust,
inverse-probability-weighted and outcome-regression versions of the
conditional assumption [@santanna-zhao-2020], applied at each threshold $y$.

**Data:** Panel data or repeated cross sections (`panel = FALSE`).

```{r}
#| label: cdf-did
#| eval: false
res_cdf <- cdf_did(
  yname  = "lemp", gname = "first.treat", tname = "year",
  idname = "countyreal", data = mpdta,
  gt_type = "qtt", probs = seq(0.1, 0.9, 0.1), biters = 100
)
autoplot(res_cdf)
```

```{r}
#| label: cdf-did-plot
#| echo: false
#| fig-alt: "Overall QTT curve from cdf_did()"
autoplot(res_cdf)
```

## Lagged-Outcome Unconfoundedness — `lou_qtt()`

**Identifying assumption:** Conditional on the pre-treatment outcome (and any
covariates $X$), untreated potential outcomes are independent of treatment:
$$Y_t(0) \perp D \mid Y_{t-1}, X.$$

**Intuition:** Treatment is as good as randomly assigned among units with
the same pre-treatment outcome. This is not a parallel trends assumption:
selection may depend on the level of the lagged outcome but, given it, not on
unobserved unit-specific heterogeneity. DiD-type assumptions instead allow
selection on time-invariant unobservables. The two are not nested, and when
they disagree it is informative to report both.
The counterfactual distribution is estimated by inverse probability
weighting, outcome (quantile) regression, or a doubly robust combination
(`est_method = c("aipw", "ipw", "reg")`).

**Data:** Panel data. With `lagged_outcome_cov = FALSE` the lagged outcome is
dropped from the conditioning set, leaving unconfoundedness given $X$, which
also works with repeated cross sections.

```{r}
#| label: lou
#| eval: false
res_lou <- lou_qtt(
  yname  = "lemp", gname = "first.treat", tname = "year",
  idname = "countyreal", data = mpdta,
  gt_type = "qtt", probs = seq(0.1, 0.9, 0.1), biters = 100
)
autoplot(res_lou)
```

```{r}
#| label: lou-plot
#| echo: false
#| fig-alt: "Overall QTT curve from lou_qtt()"
autoplot(res_lou)
```

---

## Summary

| Function | Identifying assumption | Repeated cross sections | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `cic()` | Same distributional time-change for both groups (changes-in-changes) | Yes | Needs a support condition; continuous outcomes |
| `qdid()` | Parallel trends in every quantile | Yes | Continuous outcomes |
| `panel_qtt()` | Parallel trends in the distribution of changes + copula stable over time | No | Needs ≥ 2 pre-treatment periods |
| `ddid()` | Parallel trends in the distribution of changes + same copula for both groups | No | |
| `mdid()` | Treated distribution shifts by the comparison group's mean change | Yes | Implies mean parallel trends, and is stronger |
| `cdf_did()` | Parallel trends in distribution functions | Yes | Also identified for discrete outcomes |
| `lou_qtt()` | Unconfoundedness given the lagged outcome | With `lagged_outcome_cov = FALSE` | Not a parallel trends assumption |

All seven take covariates through `xformula`. All return a `pte_qtt` object
for `gt_type = "qtt"`, or a `pte_emp_boot` object for `gt_type = "att"`,
with `summary()` and `autoplot()` methods. See
`vignette("staggered-adoption")` for the full applied workflow.
